entities.title: Design pass
entities.summary: A designer reviews and improves the browser's design, from the description of the product in this folder.
entities.details:
Everything the browser does is described in this folder's `.dev/` files, which the browser itself shows. A suggested order:

1. The [vision](.dev/vision.json) and the [stakeholders](.dev/stakeholders.json): who it is for and why.
2. The [journeys](.dev/user-journey.json) and [use cases](.dev/use-case.json): what readers set out to do, and what happens when it goes another way.
3. The [page states](.dev/page.state-diagram.json), the [token panel](.dev/token-panel.state-diagram.json) and a [drawing under the pointer](.dev/drawing.state-diagram.json): every screen and state a design has to cover, with the messages shown in each.
4. The [features](.dev/feature.json): what each part of the screen offers, with its limits.
5. The [decisions](.dev/decisions.json): the current look and the reasons for it, colours, type and icons included.
6. The [limitations](.dev/limitations.json): what readers run into today.
7. The [requirements](.dev/requirements.json), [quality requirements](.dev/quality-requirements.json) and [contracts](.dev/contracts.json): what any design must keep.

The current decisions on look and layout are where the page is now, not limits on the pass. The requirements, quality requirements and contracts hold whatever the design.

origin.description: Describe the product fully in its .dev folder so that a designer can make a good pass at it.

acceptanceCriteria: Covers every state in the three state diagrams, the landing page, refusals and empty results included.
Covers every feature on a 15-inch laptop, and makes good use of 27-inch and 34-inch and wider monitors, in light and dark.
Keeps every requirement, quality requirement and contract in this folder.

entities.title: Cyberspace: the repository in 3D
entities.summary: A second way to read a repository beside the flat page: a folder as a tower of floors, a drawn view as a city of glass towers, and a walk through it at street level.
entities.details:
The [implementation spec](docs/cyberspace-mode-spec.md) says how to build it: where the code goes in `index.html`, how a view becomes a 3D world, the exact look, the address forms, the fallbacks, the build order and the tests. The design it follows is the canvas *Cyberspace explorer in 3D*, linked from the spec and copied in [docs/cyberspace-design](docs/cyberspace-design/README.md).

The [plan](.dev/plan.json) builds it in eight pull requests and says how each is checked. It changes one recorded decision, `one-motion`, which the spec amends with a new decision `cyberspace-motion`. The questions still open are decisions: `per-entity-cities` and `cross-browser-checks`.

Done on 2026-11-15 (plan cyberspace-mode, step 8). What it delivered is described by the feature and capability *Fly through a repository in 3D*, the use case *Walk to a part and read it* and the journey *Walking through a district*, the state machine of Cyberspace's scenes, the Cyberspace group of the component diagram, decisions cyberspace-mode and cyberspace-motion, requirement works-without-webgl and quality requirement space-frame-rate. The spec's acceptance checklist passed in Chrome on that day, in the look Cyberspace was built with; its Safari and Firefox part is backlog item safari-firefox-checks, and the items for the Gibson look wait for plan cyberspace-gibson.

origin.description: Design a visual cyberspace in 3D for the explorer, then write an implementation spec for the agent that builds it, kept in the repository.

acceptanceCriteria: Everything on the spec's acceptance checklist passes for this repository in current Chrome, Safari and Firefox, in light and dark.
Without WebGL or three.js, everything is still readable in the flat view, which says why.
Every existing form of the page's address keeps its meaning; Cyberspace links opened by an older copy of the page land on the same folder and part.
Each step's pull request updates the `.dev` files for what it built, and when the last step lands the files listed in the spec's last section describe Cyberspace.

relationships.description: Amended by the new decision cyberspace-motion.
The Cyberspace group and the three.js beacon.
The acceptance checklist in Safari and Firefox, left open.

entities.title: Cyberspace in the Gibson look
entities.summary: Cyberspace always dark, like the Gibson in Hackers: cyan glass towers carrying their own record, circuit traces on a glossy black floor, arcs when lit.
entities.details:
Decision space-gibson-look says what the look is, and the [spec](docs/cyberspace-mode-spec.md)'s Rendering section how it is drawn; artboards 11 to 15 in [docs/cyberspace-design](docs/cyberspace-design/README.md) draw it. Plan cyberspace-gibson builds it in four pull requests.

Done on 2026-11-19, in four pull requests: G1 (#25, 2026-11-15), always dark, with the sky, the glossy floor, fog, the cyan glass, glowing edges and magenta beacons; G2 (#26, 2026-11-16), every relationship a circuit trace on the floor between pads, lit in place and picked on the floor; G3 (#29, 2026-11-18), every tower's faces carrying its own record, the folder tower's floors their views and the skyline's buildings their folders, all of it reflected in the floor; and G4 (2026-11-19), the selected part's relationships rising as arcs of light (one set of glow lines, one draw call, with a hidden pick tube), the fit framing what stands and the lit arcs, the street's towers within 18 units named on their faces rather than by pills, plate names glowing in their colour, the legend's `trace` and `arc` icons and words, and *traces* and *arcs* in every word a reader sees where Cyberspace said *beams*. The spec's acceptance checklist was run again in Chrome in the new look on 2026-11-19; its Safari and Firefox part stays with backlog item safari-firefox-checks. Between G2 and G3 the owner ruled that Cyberspace stays dark whatever Flat's theme switch says (#27, #28).

origin.description: Make Cyberspace always dark, styled like the Gibson in Hackers, with a design pass approved before any build.

acceptanceCriteria: Every scene looks as artboards 11 to 15 draw it, whatever the system's colour scheme, and Flat follows the system as before.
Every word on a tower's face is the part's own, and nothing moves unless the camera does.
No trace passes through a tower, for every drawn view of this repository and retro-games.
The budgets in quality requirement space-frame-rate still hold, measured with a pixel read back.

entities.title: The landing page forgets a new address after a bad one
entities.summary: After a ?url= the page can't read, Browse reloads an empty landing page instead of opening the new address.
entities.expected: Typing a good address and pressing Browse opens it.
entities.observed: The landing page reloads with an empty field. The form's submit handler and the field's focus are set up only when the page opens without ?url=, so the form submits as a plain form with no named field.

entities.title: Stand a file's use cases or journeys side by side in Cyberspace
entities.summary: A city stands one use case or journey of a file at a time, chosen by a radio button in its Layers panel; decision per-entity-cities is whether several can stand together, as tick boxes.
entities.details: What steps 6 and 7 found. Standing a file's use cases side by side needs no new rules: every city standing is placed by its bounds, 12 units right of the last (`layerOffsets`), and picked, labelled, walked and mapped by its view and part (`districtWorld`), as the folder's other views already are. What limits it is the draw-call cap. Each city standing is its own meshes, 4 to 10 draw calls (`cityCalls`: 9 for this repository's component city, 5 for a state machine), and the scene keeps 7 for the ground and the most a selection adds, so the Layers panel (`layerFits`) lets about four to six cities stand at once within the 40 calls a city scene may take: this repository's component diagram with its deployment diagram and three of its four state machines (33 calls, 40 with Loader selected and a beam under the pointer). Tick boxes for a file's use cases would work within that cap, disabled as the other views' are when one more would pass it; standing all six of this repository's use cases beside the component city would not fit. From step G2 of plan cyberspace-gibson (2026-11-16) until G3 adds each city's two reflections, a city's traces, pads and rings are one geometry of ribbons and a selection's rings and a trace under the pointer cost no call: a city takes 3 to 5 calls (5 for the component city, 3 for a state machine or a use case) and the scene keeps 4, so all six of this repository's drawn views stand together in 26 calls with Loader selected and a trace under the pointer, and six use cases beside the component city would take 27; with G3's reflections and G4's arcs, 40. Standing more would need cities merged into shared meshes, at the cost of picking, marking and fading by city, which each city now does on its own meshes.

origin.description: The spec's Records to update: a backlog item for each open question that stays open.

acceptanceCriteria: If they stand side by side: a file's use cases or journeys are tick boxes in the Layers panel, each standing as the folder's other views do, and the scene stays within 40 draw calls whatever is ticked, selected or under the pointer.

entities.title: Run Cyberspace's acceptance checklist in Safari and Firefox
entities.summary: The checklist has passed in Chrome; Safari and Firefox are unchecked until decision cross-browser-checks says who runs it there.
entities.details: The spec's acceptance checklist was run in Chrome for Testing, driven through the DevTools protocol, on 2026-11-15, and everything on it passed in the look Cyberspace was built with; the items for the Gibson look wait for plan cyberspace-gibson, whose last step runs the checklist again. The machine the work is checked on has no WebKit or Firefox build an agent can drive, so the checklist's Safari and Firefox part waits for decision cross-browser-checks: the owner runs it, or approves installing Playwright's WebKit and Firefox builds so that an agent can. Worth watching there: WebGL 2 (Safari has had it since 15), `:has()` (the ?spacestats readout steps left of an open inspector with it), `backdrop-filter`, and pointer and wheel events for orbiting, pinching and the trackpad.

origin.description: The spec's Records to update: a backlog item for each open question that stays open.

acceptanceCriteria: Every item of the spec's acceptance checklist passes in current Safari and Firefox, in light and dark, on a 15-inch laptop and a 27-inch monitor.

entities.title: Give a tower with every floor in an address of its own
entities.summary: Slide back leaves #<folder>|~space in the address, which also means the folder's first drawn view pulled out, so a reload, a shared link or Back brings a floor out again. #<folder>|view:|~space, an empty view, would say it without breaking any copy of the page.
entities.details:
Found in step 8, in Chrome on 2026-11-15.

Today, Slide back replaces the history entry with `#<folder>|~space` and keeps every floor in only while the reader stays (`space.shut`). Reloaded, `#|~space` pulls the component diagram out again; after the reader moves on, Back to that entry stands the tower with whatever floor the tower had out. So the address doesn't hold what the reader sees, as decision address-is-state asks.

An empty view is the form to use:

- Today's Flat reads `#<folder>|view:` as `#<folder>`: `focusPart` finds no section with an empty file name and leaves the folder as it opened (checked on the root and on `worker`). A copy of the page from before Cyberspace reads it the same way (its `focusPart` is the same), and ignores the `|~space` after it.
- Today's Cyberspace reads `#<folder>|view:|~space` as `#<folder>|~space`: `towerAsk` finds no floor with an empty file name and asks for nothing, so a fresh load pulls the first drawn view out, and a tower already standing keeps the floor it has out (checked on the root and on `worker`).

So no copy of the page misreads it, and the grammar needs no new segment. The change would be: `towerAsk` reads an empty `view:` as no floor out, `towerSlideBack` writes `#<folder>|view:|~space`, contract page-address gains the form, and test/space.test.js a row. `#<folder>|~space` keeps its meaning, the first drawn view out. If the owner would rather a slid-back tower stay a passing state, nothing is needed: the tower is the same either way, and only the drawer differs.

origin.description: Step 7's session suggested the empty view; step 8 checked what today's page does with it.

acceptanceCriteria: After Slide back the address is #<folder>|view:|~space, and reloading it, or coming back to it with Back or Forward, stands the tower with every floor in.
#<folder>|~space still pulls the folder's first drawn view out, and #<folder>|view: still opens the folder in Flat.
